papers.title_in_file: Suppressing unwanted fluctuations in QAOA and approximate quantum annealing
papers.version_note: arXiv:2212.00515v1, 1 Dec 2022 (dated 2 December 2022 on the first page). Text is the preprint only; no second copy.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation and small IonQ Harmony study of scaling per-qubit QAOA/AQA mixer angles by diagonal Fubini-Study metric elements (suppressed and thresholded mixers) to reduce fluctuation-driven trapping in false minima.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Grover, that quantum computers have a provable advantage over any possible quantum technique in searching an unstructured search space.
quotes: It was shown by Grover [1] that quantum computers have a provable advantage over any possible quantum technique in searching an unstructured search space.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that near term devices can only implement algorithms of limited depth due to noise, so heuristic techniques that do not require deep circuits are important to consider.
quotes: Since near term devices are only going to be able to implement algorithms of limited depth due to noise, it is important to consider heuristic techniques which do not require deep circuits to operate.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors describe approximate quantum annealing (AQA, a term coined by Willsch et al.) as a non-variational algorithm based on choosing parameters which simulate a quantum anneal.
quotes: an additional algorithm, known as approximate quantum annealing (AQA) [8], which is a non-variational algorithm based on choosing parameters which simulate a quantum anneal.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines AQA in its own introduction (Section 1, p.2).

assertions.value: The authors state that their use of the Fubini-Study metric differs from quantum natural gradients, where the pseudo-inverse of the Fubini-Study metric is employed as geometric preconditioning of the gradient descent update.
quotes: Our use of the Fubini-Study metric diﬀers from previous uses for example quantum natural gradients, where the pseudo-inverse of the Fubini-Study metric is employed as geometric preconditioning of the gradient descent update [16].
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of their own use of the metric in Section 1, p.2.

assertions.value: The authors report that recent investigations suggest geometry-aware preconditioning outperforms other gradient and non gradient based optimisation methods, with the overhead of computing second order derivatives.
quotes: Recent investigations [17, 18] suggest this geometry-aware preconditioning outperforms other, gradient and non gradient based, optimisation methods (with the overhead of computing second order derivatives).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike AQA, QAOA requires many repetitions of the protocols to find the optimal gamma and beta and incurs substantial numerical overhead.
quotes: Unlike AQA, QAOA requires many repetitions of the protocols to ﬁnd the optimal γ and β and incurs substantial numerical overhead.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors define their simple AQA protocol as approximating a linear anneal, with the angles chosen such that the sum of gamma and beta for every layer equals tau, and so that no iteration is trivial with gamma or beta equal to zero.
quotes: Note that the values have been chosen such that γl + βl = τ
we never have a “trivial” iteration where γl = 0 or βl = 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the paper's own AQA schedule, Section 2.1, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use a first order Trotterisation in their AQA so that it is a closer analog to a QAOA protocol, and they would expect similar results for the second-order method used by Willsch et al.
quotes: we use a ﬁrst order Trotterisation, although we would expect it to ﬁnd similar results for the second-order method used in [8].
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of their own method setup, Section 2.1, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that by the adiabatic theorem the probability of finding an optimal solution will tend toward 1 as p tends to infinity for their AQA scaling of tau with p, a guarantee which does not exist for fixed tau.
quotes: By the adiabatic theorem of quantum mechanics, it follows that the probability of ﬁnding an optimal solution will tend toward 1 as p tends toward ∞, a theoretical guarantee which does not exist for ﬁxed τ .
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper invokes the adiabatic theorem without a proof of its own; the guarantee rests on the stated scaling of tau with p and on the standard theorem.

assertions.value: The authors choose tau of p to equal pi divided by two times p to the power 0.25, a relatively simple polynomial dependence on p.
quotes: we choose a relatively simple polynomial dependence:
individual angles are decreased τ (p) = . π 2p0.25
assertions.certainty_reason: The schedule used throughout the paper is stated in Section 2.1 and again in Section 7.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the fraction flat; reading it as pi over two p to the 0.25 is the reader's reconstruction of the layout.

assertions.value: The paper derives that for the non-uniform mixer state, the diagonal Fubini-Study element equals one minus the square of the expectation of X on that qubit.
quotes: Let us consider the simple case of a state operated upon by a non-uniform mixer term
Fj,j(ζ) = 1 − ( ψ|Xj|ψ )2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from Eqs. 10-13 in Section 2.2; the statement and its condition (the non-uniform mixer state of Eq. 11) are quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The exponent on the expectation is printed flat as 2 in the text layer; it is a square.

assertions.value: The authors state that the elements of the metric can all be readily obtained through simple X basis measurements of the state.
quotes: These quantities can all be readily obtained through simple X basis measurements of the state
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Stated as following from Eq. 13; the paper gives no separate resource analysis of the measurement cost.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the state is an eigenstate of X on a qubit, the operation on that qubit is only a global phase projected out in the definition of the metric, so the diagonal and all off-diagonal elements for that parameter are zero.
quotes: In this case, the action of the operation is only a global phase which is projected out in the deﬁnition of the metric.
the diagonal and all possible oﬀ-diagonal elements of the metric corresponding to this ζj will be zero
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in Section 2.2, p.6 with its condition (the state is an eigenstate of X on that qubit) and said to be verifiable from Eq. 13.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the starting state is an eigenstate no mixing between computational basis states is performed, and that the rotation can actually be harmful to the computation.
quotes: no mixing between computational basis states is performed by setting ζj = 0.
Beyond just not being useful, this rotation can actually be harmful to the computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the example state of the preceding equation (mostly in an X eigenstate on one qubit with a small component in the zero state) the diagonal-element formula gives a result for which the amount of mixing the operation performs is minimal.
quotes: By applying Eq. 14, we ﬁnd that Fj,j = 2, so the amount of mixing which this operation performs is minimal.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints Fj,j = 2, which cannot be the value of a quantity that Eq. 14 bounds above by one; a symbol (probably a small parameter squared) was probably lost in the layer. The paper's printed value is not relied on.

assertions.value: The authors state that applying the driver term to such a state has a desirable effect of performing a bit flip on the component that is not an eigenstate, and an undesirable effect of applying a relative phase to the two components; they state this phase mimics the phase separator and could favor a suboptimal basis state over the optimal one, globally corrupting the computation.
quotes: an undesirable eﬀect of applying a relative phase to the two components
it will lead to phase interference which could favor a suboptimal computational basis state over the truly optimal one and therefore could globally corrupt the computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors define the suppressed mixer by setting each mixer angle zeta of j proportional to the diagonal Fubini-Study element for qubit j, normalised by the largest diagonal element so that the maximum value of elements in zeta is 1, using the previous stage's metric values to set the current stage's angles.
quotes: The simple protocol we propose is to scale each ζj proportional to Fj,j(ζ).
we constrain that the maximum value of elements in ζ to be 1
we estimate the ζj values for a given stage by using the values of Fj,j from the previous stage.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the paper's own protocol, Section 3, p.7.

assertions.value: The authors define the thresholded mixer: first run the circuit without any modifications, and only modify a qubit's mixer angle if its final diagonal Fubini-Study element for the unmodified run is below a threshold; they report that a threshold of 0.2 works well empirically and use it throughout.
quotes: We additionally consider a version of the protocol where we ﬁrst run the circuit without any modiﬁcations
Empirically, we ﬁnd that Θ = 0.2 works well as a threshold, so we use that throughout the analysis presented here.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the paper's own protocol and its fixed threshold, Section 3, p.8.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not show a sweep over the threshold; the statement that 0.2 works well is empirical.

assertions.value: The authors call the traditional QAOA protocol and its AQA analog, where the relative strength of the individual mixer terms is not changed, the unmodified mixer.
quotes: We refer to the traditional QAOA protocol (and its AQA analog) where the relative strength of the individual mixer terms is not changed using an unmodiﬁed mixer.
assertions.certainty_reason: Naming definition stated in Section 3, p.8.

assertions.value: The authors state that an established trick in quantum annealing experiments is to use Ising Hamiltonians with free variables, engineered to have a low energy state where many variables yield equal energy for the zero or one configuration, and that this creates a very close avoided crossing.
quotes: An established trick in quantum annealing experiments is to use Ising Hamiltonians, which contain
This design creates a very close avoided crossing, as the system must tunnel from the low energy state to the true ground state late in the anneal.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use the 16 qubit problem from Dickson et al. and also an 8 qubit QUBO inspired by the Hamiltonian studied by Boixo et al.
quotes: we use the 16 qubit problem from [19]
We also investigate an 8 qubit QUBO inspired by the Hamiltonian studied in [20]
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4, p.8 states which test problems the paper uses.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in contrast to quantum annealing with moderate runtimes, which gives a probability approaching unity of being in the false minimum, low to moderate depth AQA gives a probability on the order of 50% for the sixteen qubit problem.
quotes: low to moderate depth AQA only results in a probability on the order of 50% (see results section)
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement is made in passing before the results section; the numerical result is plotted in Figure 7b, whose axis values the text layer does not carry.

assertions.value: The authors report that changing the diagonal QUBO elements to reduce the difference between the false minima and the true minima by a factor of 5 creates a problem in which the tendency to get trapped in a false minima is much stronger.
quotes: by changing the diagonal QUBO elements in a way which reduces the diﬀerence between the false minima and the true minima by a factor of 5
assertions.certainty_reason: Construction of the modified test problem, Section 4, p.8.

assertions.value: The authors state that the engineered true and false minima problems do not generally have the typical structure of hard optimisation problems, and, since they only have negative off-diagonal elements, are not likely to have the complex landscape of false minima present in real hard combinatorial optimisation problems.
quotes: do not generally have any of the typical structure of hard optimisation problems.
they are not likely to have the complex landscape of false minima which is present in real, hard combinatorial optimisation problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of the first two test problems in Section 4, p.9.

assertions.value: The authors state that they couple a false-minimum gadget to a weighted maximum cut problem, which is symmetric under inversion of all bits by construction, so that one of the two equivalent solutions is the true minimum and the other a false minimum.
quotes: we need to couple a gadget similar to the ones shown in ﬁgure 2b to a hard problem which is symmetric under full bit inversion.
this problem is symmetric under inversion of all bits by construction.
assertions.certainty_reason: Construction of the specialised QUBO, Section 4, p.9.

assertions.value: The authors give an algorithm to generate the test problems: it initialises a QUBO of size ncut + 2ngadget, builds a random weighted maximum cut part, solves it by exhaustive search for the small instances used, couples it to the gadget, and adds a bias so that the true minimum has lower energy than the false minimum.
quotes: Initialize empty QUBO Q of size ncut + 2ngadget
This QUBO is then solved on line 12 for the small instances used here. We used exhaustive search to accomplish this.
a bias is introduced so that the true minima, corresponding to the bitstring deﬁned by Sol, followed by all zeros has a lower energy than the false minima
assertions.certainty_reason: Problem-generation procedure defined in Section 4, p.9-11.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the qubits of free variables take the plus configuration, the state acquires an additional phase rotation of minus beta from the mixer for each such qubit, and that they base their intuition on the phases a state acquires when the phase separator and mixer are applied sequentially, since there is no obvious natural spectral gap for QAOA.
quotes: there is not an obvious natural notion of spectral gap for QAOA
We instead base our intuition on the phases a state acquires when the phase separator and mixer are performed sequentially
then the state will acquire an additional −β of phase rotation from the mixer operation for each qubit in this conﬁguration.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors define the phase of a state under one QAOA layer as the argument of the expectation of the single layer unitary in that state, with a branch cut at pi and gamma and beta limited so the phase magnitude does not exceed pi.
quotes: where U (γ, β) is the unitary deﬁned by a single layer of the QAOA circuit, equation 5, and |ψ is the state it is applied to.
we consider a branch cut at π
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition stated in Section 5, p.12.

Experiments were performed on an IonQ Harmony device in October 2022.
For each point we performed 10 separate experimental runs with 100 samples each

assertions.value: The authors report that for the original sixteen qubit problem under the linear protocol none of the diagonal Fubini-Study elements fall below the threshold of 0.2 for the p values examined, so the thresholded and unmodified protocols are equivalent for this problem.
quotes: the diagonal elements of the Fubini-Study metric ever fall below Θ = 0.2 for
Because the diagonal metric elements never fall below the threshold, the thresholded and unmodiﬁed protocols are equivalent for this problem.

assertions.value: The authors report that for both the suppressed and unmodified mixer there is a general trend of increasing success probability with increasing p on the original problem, that the false minimum probability trends upward for the unmodified mixer but stays far from unity, and that the suppressed mixer reverses the trend at p of about 15 (the relation sign is lost in the text layer).
quotes: there is a general trend of increasing success probability with increasing p.
but one which is far from unity for the p values we examine.
We do see that the suppressed mixer reverses the trend at p 15, suggesting that the suppression is acting as desired.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Single problem instance; the suppressed mixer's effect on success probability is not stated as a gain in the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the modified problem with a reduced separation, a diabatic bump is clearly visible for the unmodified version, that the success probabilities for the two modified-driver protocols oscillate with increasing p, and that the success probability for the unmodified mixer drops dramatically as p is increased.
quotes: a feature known as a “diabatic bump”
the success probability corresponding to the unmodiﬁed mixer drops dramatically as p is increased.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the modified problem shows a high probability to find the false minimum and that at large p this probability is higher for the unmodified mixer.
quotes: this problem also shows a high probability for the false minimum to be found, and at large p, this probability is higher for the unmodiﬁed mixer.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the modified-problem example does not directly demonstrate an advantage from suppressing fluctuations, since peak performance is reached at relatively low p, before the threshold for suppression on any qubit is reached; they state the suppressed and thresholded mixers do raise the final diagonal Fubini-Study elements of the variables that are free in the local minimum.
quotes: This example problem, however, does not directly demonstrate an advantage from suppressing ﬂuctuations since peak performance is reached at relatively low p
the ﬁnal values of the diagonal elements of the Fubini-Study metric corresponding to the variables which are free in the local minimum can be signiﬁcantly increased using these techniques.

assertions.value: The authors test a specialised QUBO from Algorithm 1 with ncut = 6, ngadget = 4, Jgadget = 0.25, Jcouple = 0.5, Bias = 1.5, whose weighted maximum cut part creates rough features in the landscape similar to a real-world optimisation problem.
quotes: We examine a version with ncut = 6, ngadget = 4, Jgadget = 0.25, Jcouple = 0.5, Bias = 1.5.
assertions.certainty_reason: Test instance parameters stated in Section 7.3, p.19.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the specialised QUBO the thresholded and suppressed methods both significantly outperform an unmodified mixer, with the thresholded technique performing the best, and a general upward trend in success probability with increasing p.
quotes: The thresholded and suppressed methods both signiﬁcantly outperform an unmodiﬁed mixer, with the thresholded technique performing the best, and a general upward trend in success probability with increasing p.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical or author-stated result of one study.
assertions.reader_inference: One instance for this statement; the multi-instance check is in the next assertion.

assertions.value: The authors report that at p = 24 a more traditional QAOA strategy performs somewhat worse than traditional AQA with a linear schedule, and explain that the QAOA optimisation targets energy expectation rather than success probability, and the false minimum also has a low energy expectation.

optimises against energy expectation, rather than the actual success probability

optimisation with each run consisting of 300 iterations.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the specialised QUBO the cases where the true minimum is not found are not dominated by the false minimum, that the false minimum probability is relatively small and starts dropping off beyond p of about 15, and that the thresholded mixer leads only to a small decrease in the false minimum probability.

the thresholded mixer only leads to a small decrease in the probability to be found in the false minimum.

assertions.value: The authors suggest, as a likely explanation, that the system ends the evolution in more complex states that still exhibit strong single qubit fluctuations on a subset of the qubits, since the final diagonal elements are increased by the suppressed and thresholded strategies.

assertions.value: The authors report that, especially at higher p, modification of the mixer leads to much better performance; at the lowest p the thresholded and suppressed strategies look comparable, as p is increased there is a clear separation for all difficulties in favor of the thresholded method, and at p = 50 the lowest success probability instance performs better than the best instance under the unmodified protocol.

there is a clear separation for all diﬃculties of problems in favor of the thresholded method.

assertions.value: The authors report that, from the later size-comparison figures, the separation in performance seems to scale as a function of size, with the effect becoming more pronounced as the problem QUBOs become bigger.
quotes: the separation in performance seems to scale as a function of size with the eﬀect becoming more pronounced as the problem QUBOs become bigger.
